text: {"thinking":"The manufacturer confirms delivery of 2,000 GPUs. I’ll compare that count and the serial ranges with the operator’s system list to identify any hardware that needs independent follow-up.","action":"system_list","args":{}}

{"thinking":"Compare the operator’s system list with the manufacturer’s record of 2,000 delivered GPUs. Any discrepancy is a lead to check against grid energy and sealed scheduler records.","action":"system_list","args":{}}

{"thinking":"The listed clusters account for all 2,000 shipped GPUs by count. Check independent hourly energy across all 30 days for sustained loads or unexplained demand, then use those periods to target checks that distinguish training from inference.","action":"utility_energy","args":{"first_day":1,"last_day":30}}

{"thinking":"The listed clusters account for all 2,000 GPUs in the manufacturer’s shipment records. I’ll use the sealed scheduler history to identify job windows, overlapping allocations and gaps, then target independent measurements where they can best distinguish one coordinated run from separate workloads.","action":"log_escrow","args":{}}

{"thinking":"The listed clusters account for all 2,000 GPUs in the manufacturer’s delivery record. Get the grid operator’s energy data for all 30 days to identify sustained loads and test whether site consumption fits the listed capacity.","action":"utility_energy","args":{"first_day":1,"last_day":30}}

{"thinking":"The listed GPU count matches the manufacturer's shipment total. Check the grid operator's energy records for sustained load that could support a large training run, several independent jobs, or batch inference. Use those periods to guide later checks against the sealed scheduler logs and network measurements.","action":"utility_energy","args":{"first_day":1,"last_day":30}}

{"thinking":"The grid meter shows separate load increases on F1 on days 6–11 and F2 on days 17–19. Check the sealed scheduler records for job timing, GPU allocations, and customer labels during both periods. The records can guide independent tests of whether those loads came from training or batch inference.","action":"log_escrow","args":{}}

{"thinking":"The escrow confirms that all 30 daily logs were received and match the current copies. Read the scheduler entries to identify GPU allocations, job durations, and customer labels during the metered load increases on F1 and F2. Use those details to target independent checks for coordination and workload type.","action":"scheduler_log","args":{"first_day":1,"last_day":30}}

{"thinking":"Meridian’s batch job is large enough to breach the threshold if it was a single training run. I’ll sample Cluster A on day 16, midway through the allocation, to see whether GPU-to-GPU traffic is consistent with batch inference, low-communication training, or ordinary training.","action":"interconnect_tap","args":{"link":"A","day":16}}

{"thinking":"Outbound traffic rose during the F1 increase on days 15–16 and stayed near baseline during the earlier power increases. Check the sealed daily logs for job allocations, durations, and labels that can guide independent tests of training and coordination.","action":"log_escrow","args":{}}

{"thinking":"Cluster A’s day 16 traffic was about 10 MB/s per GPU, consistent with low-communication training and roughly 1,000 times the stated inference baseline. I’ll check F1 for a training-like power signature on the same day. A periodic line can also come from batch inference or cooling, and one day of traffic leaves the run’s duration unresolved.","action":"power_spectrum","args":{"feed":"F1","day":16}}

{"thinking":"Day 16’s traffic supports low-communication training, while the absent power line leaves both irregular training and batch inference plausible. I’ll check independent grid records for sustained load across Meridian’s eight-day allocation and for unexplained demand elsewhere in the month. The grid data can corroborate duration, but it cannot identify a coordinated run on its own.","action":"utility_energy","args":{"first_day":1,"last_day":30}}

{"thinking":"Five explanations remain plausible. Separate short fine-tunes can be checked against customer records and interconnect traffic. Batch inference can be checked with the tap and live chip probes. A larger run omitted from the logs or split across labels can be checked with feed spectra and cross-cluster traffic. Unlisted capacity can be checked against inventory and grid readings. Missing logs or late payments can be checked against escrow and bank records, which so far show no such gaps. Start with F1 on day 12, when the scheduler records no job, to look for a periodic load in the steady baseline.","action":"power_spectrum","args":{"feed":"F1","day":12}}

{"thinking":"Tidewater confirmed its order, and the day 8 tap measured aggregate traffic without showing whether the two GPU groups exchanged data. The allocations total 50,400 GPU-hours only if they served one training process. Check Ostara Legal’s registration and whether it independently confirms its fine-tuning order.","action":"customer_check","args":{"customer":"Ostara Legal"}}

{"thinking":"The balance check skipped days 11–13. Escrow records only interactive inference on those days, and the independent tap found traffic inside A on day 12 consistent with low-communication training. Read the full scheduler log to identify allocations before and after the gap and see whether declared jobs could be stages of one run. Use those records to target independent checks of continuity and coordination.","action":"scheduler_log","args":{"first_day":1,"last_day":30}}

{"thinking":"The grid records corroborate sustained load on A during Meridian’s allocation and a shorter load on B during Ostara’s fine-tune. I’ll run the fixed balance checks to see whether the recorded allocations account for the metered energy and to identify discrepancies worth testing with independent measurements.","action":"balance_checks","args":{}}

{"thinking":"The balance check flagged lower outbound traffic on days 11–15 and higher traffic on days 16–20. The five-day totals obscure whether the changes align with Meridian’s allocation on days 12–19. I’ll check the ISP’s daily records to see whether ordinary demand shifts can explain the pattern and to choose days for follow-up interconnect samples.","action":"outbound_traffic","args":{"first_day":1,"last_day":30}}

{"thinking":"Tidewater and Ostara independently confirmed their orders and paid from their own accounts. That supports separate jobs, while the day 8 tap measured only aggregate traffic. Switch to the independent power sensor on F1 during the overlap. If it resolves two periodic signatures, compare them with days when each allocation ran alone.","action":"power_spectrum","args":{"feed":"F1","day":8}}

{"thinking":"F1 showed one periodic line during Tidewater’s solo window and two during the overlap. Check day 10, when only Ostara’s fine-tune was logged, to see whether its solo signature can account for one of the overlap lines after allowing for frequency drift.","action":"power_spectrum","args":{"feed":"F1","day":10}}

{"thinking":"The first probe reached only the first five requested GPUs, leaving the higher-numbered nodes unchecked. Probe those nodes at hour 660 to test whether the unusual day 28 traffic coincided with training, inference, or idle readings on the chips presented.","action":"chip_probe","args":{"nodes":["A-0700","A-0800","A-0900","A-1000","A-1150"],"hour":660}}

{"thinking":"F1 showed no periodic line on days 12 and 16, even though GPU-to-GPU traffic on both days was consistent with low-communication training. I’ll check day 14, when the feed was under sustained load and outbound traffic was near baseline. A line would add evidence for intermittent training, though periodic batch inference remains possible. Either result leaves the run’s GPU count and continuity unresolved.","action":"power_spectrum","args":{"feed":"F1","day":14}}

{"thinking":"Escrow confirms the operator presented the same logs it filed each day. Read the scheduler entries to identify workloads, GPU counts, and possible job splits behind the F1 load on days 20–28 and the F2 load on days 9–10. Use those entries to target independent checks for training, batch inference, and coordination.","action":"scheduler_log","args":{"first_day":1,"last_day":30}}

{"thinking":"The day 28 A–B tap measured traffic consistent with low-communication training, but it cannot show whether both clusters belonged to one run or how many GPUs participated. Follow the billing lead through the bank. Check whether the flagged Lumen Health invoice reflects a late or partial payment, and look for payment records tied to workloads missing from the scheduler.","action":"bank_payments","args":{}}

{"thinking":"The ISP records confirm a day 19 spike consistent with a bulk download, while the optical tap still showed traffic characteristic of low-communication training. The bank records may identify who paid for bt-0431 and whether the payment reference supports the document-labeling account. The balance check only established that invoices were paid.","action":"bank_payments","args":{}}

{"thinking":"Day 26 traffic strongly favors training over ordinary batch inference, but one day cannot establish the run’s total GPU-hours. Sample cluster A on day 20, when the sustained F1 load began, to test whether training-scale communication was already present.","action":"interconnect_tap","args":{"link":"A","day":20}}

{"thinking":"The bank confirms that Northwind Apps paid EUR 150,000, but the scheduler lists no job under its name. Lumen Health has an unpaid invoice for the same amount. Northwind's payment could cover ordinary inference or a workload missing from the scheduler. Check its registration and ask what service it purchased and when it ran.","action":"customer_check","args":{"customer":"Northwind Apps"}}

{"thinking":"Training-scale traffic on days 20 and 26 challenges the batch label. A live probe on day 27 can test whether chips across the recorded allocation show training or inference signatures. Include a chip from the interactive pool for comparison. The probe cannot establish run membership or duration.","action":"chip_probe","args":{"nodes":["A-0250","A-0501","A-0600","A-0700","A-0800","A-0900","A-1000","A-1100","A-1200"],"hour":636}}

{"thinking":"Lumen Health’s unpaid invoice has no matching scheduled job. It could reflect a late payment for ordinary inference, or it could point to an unrecorded workload. Check Lumen’s registration and ask what service it ordered, when it ran, and whether it used both clusters. The invoice amount alone does not establish a link to Northwind’s payment or the traffic measured on day 28.","action":"customer_check","args":{"customer":"Lumen Health"}}

{"thinking":"The day 26 spectrum showed a steady 0.93 Hz line. Check F1 on day 20, when the tap also measured training-scale traffic, to see whether a similar signature was present at the start of the load plateau. A match would support continuity across the two dates, while separate training runs or periodic equipment could also produce similar lines.","action":"power_spectrum","args":{"feed":"F1","day":20}}

{"thinking":"Both GPU feeds show sustained elevated load on days 22–27 and a partial return to baseline on day 28. Check the sealed scheduler logs for recorded allocations and timing. Use those records to target independent checks that can distinguish one coordinated run from separate jobs or batch inference.","action":"log_escrow","args":{}}

{"thinking":"Training signatures and heavy GPU traffic challenge the batch label. One sustained run, several shorter runs, unusual batch inference, and a periodic cooling controller remain competing explanations. Run the fixed balance checks to reconcile the recorded allocations with metered energy and identify any gaps before testing continuity across days 20–28.","action":"balance_checks","args":{}}

{"thinking":"The day 28 probes classified the presented chips as inference or idle. The tap readings still leave the GPU count, duration, and run identity unresolved. Check the declared Kestrel Search batch job on day 15, when F1 load rose. Traffic substantially above the 0.01 GB/s per GPU seen on days 12 and 28 would strengthen the case for training during that window. A similar reading would leave the batch label plausible while the source of the elevated traffic remains uncertain.","action":"interconnect_tap","args":{"link":"A","day":15}}

{"thinking":"All 30 escrow copies match the current logs. Check the recorded job types, GPU counts, and timing to identify which allocations could account for the rise on both feeds during days 22–28. Use those allocations to target independent checks for training and coordination.","action":"scheduler_log","args":{"first_day":1,"last_day":30}}

{"thinking":"Inspect daily outbound traffic around the day 15 load increase and on days 12 and 28. The five-day balance check could mask daily deviations. Traffic that tracks declared inference would support that explanation, while a sustained load increase with little change in outbound traffic would leave both batch inference and low-communication training plausible. The tap readings alone cannot establish the size or duration of a coordinated run.","action":"outbound_traffic","args":{"first_day":1,"last_day":30}}

{"thinking":"The balance check flagged a drop in outbound traffic. Get the provider’s daily totals to see whether the drop starts and ends with the F1 load plateau on days 20–28. A matching window would support the training explanation, though batch inference that stores results locally could also send little traffic.","action":"outbound_traffic","args":{"first_day":1,"last_day":30}}

{"thinking":"Grid records show sustained elevated load on both GPU feeds on days 5–16 and a smaller rise on F1 on days 20–21. Check the sealed scheduler records for allocations and timing that could distinguish a split training run, independent jobs, and batch inference. Use those records to target independent measurements.","action":"log_escrow","args":{}}

{"thinking":"The manufacturer records 2,600 GPUs delivered to Eemshaven. Compare the operator's declared systems and serial ranges with those shipments. Any gap could reflect spare, retired, or transferred GPUs, or an unlisted cluster. Use independent energy and network evidence to test those explanations.","action":"system_list","args":{}}

{"thinking":"The manufacturer records 2,600 GPUs delivered, and the operator lists 2,000 GPU nodes. The 600-unit gap could reflect spares, transfers, or unlisted equipment. Request independent grid readings for all 30 days and compare feed-level readings, if available, with declared capacity and F3’s stated cooling and storage use.","action":"utility_energy","args":{"first_day":1,"last_day":30}}

{"thinking":"Both GPU feeds show sustained elevated load on days 5–16, with no corresponding scheduler entry. The day 20–21 rise on F1 coincides with the logged Kestrel batch job. Sample the A–B interconnect on day 12 for evidence of cross-cluster coordination. The traffic measurement can help distinguish a shared run from independent workloads, while GPU count and duration still need verification.","action":"interconnect_tap","args":{"link":"A-B","day":12}}

{"thinking":"Cluster A carried training-scale traffic on days 20, 23, and 26, and F1 showed a steady line on each of those days. The gaps leave room for several shorter runs. Check day 21 for a full-day line near 0.88 Hz, consistent with the observed drift. A break or additional lines would weaken the case for one sustained run. At the recorded allocation of 700 GPUs, a single run would cross 50,000 GPU-hours in just under 72 hours.","action":"power_spectrum","args":{"feed":"F1","day":21}}

{"thinking":"Both checked customers share an address and director with Borealis Compute Holding, so their replies provide limited corroboration of separate runs. Check F1 on day 26 for periodic signatures across the four recorded fine-tunes. The same-day pattern on F2 can then help test whether the cross-cluster traffic came from one coordinated run or several independent jobs with inaccurate placement records.","action":"power_spectrum","args":{"feed":"F1","day":26}}

{"thinking":"The optical tap found substantial GPU-to-GPU traffic between clusters on days 5 and 12. Check day 16, the last day of elevated load on both feeds, to see whether cross-cluster activity persisted through the apparent end of the episode. These samples alone cannot establish that one run used more than 50,000 GPU-hours.","action":"interconnect_tap","args":{"link":"A-B","day":16}}

{"thinking":"A single coordinated run could produce the 0.87 Hz line on both feeds. Different signatures would favor separate workloads, while a matching line would strengthen the coordination hypothesis alongside the measured GPU traffic between clusters. Separate jobs or periodic equipment could still produce similar lines.","action":"power_spectrum","args":{"feed":"F2","day":26}}

{"thinking":"The balance checks flag unexplained load on both feeds across days 5–16. The optical tap favors training, while one long run and several shorter runs remain possible. Use day 12, when measured cross-cluster traffic was highest, to look for an F1 power signature that can be compared across feeds and days.","action":"power_spectrum","args":{"feed":"F1","day":12}}

{"thinking":"Escrow confirms the logs were preserved as submitted. The resale and F3 equipment remain unverified, so return to independent physical measurements. Check F3 on day 3, when the sustained load began, to see whether a line resembling day 26’s was already present. A recurring line would support a persistent workload or controller, with training and batch inference both still possible.","action":"power_spectrum","args":{"feed":"F3","day":3}}

{"thinking":"On day 12, both feeds showed steady lines near 0.88 Hz while the optical tap measured substantial GPU-to-GPU traffic between clusters. Check F1 on day 5, the first day of elevated load, for a similar signature. A match would support continuity, although successive runs using the same configuration could produce similar lines.","action":"power_spectrum","args":{"feed":"F1","day":5}}

{"thinking":"Grid load stayed elevated on both feeds from days 5–16, and the tap found substantial cross-cluster traffic at the start, middle, and end. One sustained training run and several successive runs could both explain those observations. Check F1 on day 9, inside the longest gap between spectrum samples, for a day-long line, a break, or a change in signature.","action":"power_spectrum","args":{"feed":"F1","day":9}}

{"thinking":"The declared jobs do not overlap. F3 remains the strongest lead: its sustained load and recurring power line fit training, batch inference, or periodic facility equipment. Staff addressed the resale but left F3 access unanswered. Request direct inspection during the elevated load so the verifier can trace the feed and select any GPUs for probing.","action":"staff","args":{"question":"Can you give the verifier access to trace F3 from its distribution panel to the equipment drawing power on day 27 and, if it feeds GPUs, let the verifier select nodes for a live cable probe? Please identify any equipment or racks the verifier cannot inspect."}}

{"thinking":"F3 could have powered a single training run, several independent runs, batch inference, or the cooling and storage equipment staff described. Cable tracing and a live chip probe could identify GPU workloads, while job and interconnect evidence could test coordination. The reported resale could also be genuine with payment still pending, so the bank records leave it unresolved. Use day 28 as a control: F3 returned to baseline that day. If the same line persisted, it would weaken the link between the line and the extra load. If it disappeared, it would tie the line to the load without identifying the equipment.","action":"power_spectrum","args":{"feed":"F3","day":28}}

{"thinking":"All four checked customers share an address and director with Borealis Compute Holding, and none gave a workload-specific account. The independent traffic and power measurements suggest coordination across clusters but cannot assign GPU-hours to one process. Check Brightwater AI for independent ownership and an account of what ran and where. A specific account could help distinguish a separate fine-tune from a label for part of a shared run.","action":"customer_check","args":{"customer":"Brightwater AI"}}

{"thinking":"The ISP records show that outbound traffic stayed flat through the F1 load increase. Both internal batch inference and training could explain that. Check F1 on day 23, when the tap measured 6.1 GB/s inside cluster A, for a periodic signal consistent with training. Batch inference and cooling can also produce a line, so this check alone cannot establish run size or continuity.","action":"power_spectrum","args":{"feed":"F1","day":23}}

{"thinking":"F1 shows sustained elevated load on days 8–19. The sealed scheduler records can show whether Borealis recorded one job, several jobs, or gaps during that period. Use those entries to choose where to test for training and coordination independently.","action":"log_escrow","args":{}}

{"thinking":"The day-15 tap measured about 10 MB/s per GPU on sampled A links, consistent with low-communication training and well above typical inference traffic. The sample cannot attribute that traffic to Kestrel’s job. Check Kestrel’s registration and ask what workload it commissioned. The declared allocation was 9,600 GPU-hours, so reclassifying that job alone would not breach the threshold. The tap did not cover F3.","action":"customer_check","args":{"customer":"Kestrel Search"}}

{"thinking":"Run the fixed balance checks on the scheduler allocation and utility records. The logged job exceeds 50,000 GPU-hours if it was a single training run. Both batch inference and training could explain the sustained load, so follow up with independent interconnect measurements.","action":"balance_checks","args":{}}

{"thinking":"Three of eight sampled GPUs in A’s scheduled pool read as training across days 26 and 28. The limited samples cannot establish how many GPUs trained or which run they belonged to. Measure cluster A’s peer traffic on day 28, when two GPUs read as training. Elevated traffic would independently corroborate late training activity, while inference-level traffic would weaken the case that the day 23 activity persisted. Either result leaves the size of any single run unresolved.","action":"interconnect_tap","args":{"link":"A","day":28}}

{"thinking":"Kestrel’s registration and payment support a genuine customer relationship. Its lack of a reply leaves the day-15 workload unclassified. The strongest unresolved lead is F3. Request a live probe during the elevated load on day 27, identifying the requested GPUs by manufacturer serial because staff supplied no node mapping. A probe on a GPU verified to draw from F3 could distinguish training from inference on that chip. Run coordination and duration would still need separate evidence.","action":"chip_probe","args":{"nodes":["SN102001","SN102300","SN102600"],"hour":636}}

{"thinking":"Grid records show sustained extra load on F1 during days 18–28 and a shorter rise on F2 during days 9–10. Check the sealed scheduler logs for allocations that could explain both periods, including one run split across labels, independent jobs, or batch inference. Use those allocations to target independent workload checks.","action":"log_escrow","args":{}}

{"thinking":"Escrow confirms the scheduler records were filed on time and match the current copies. Read the allocations to see what the operator recorded for the F1 surge on days 18–28 and the F2 rise on days 9–10, then use those details to target independent workload checks.","action":"scheduler_log","args":{"first_day":1,"last_day":30}}

{"thinking":"The grid confirms sustained extra load on F1 during days 18–28, when the scheduler records a 700-GPU internal batch job. Batch inference fits the power pattern. Sample Cluster A’s interconnect on day 27 to test whether its peer traffic is closer to inference or training, including training designed to exchange less data.","action":"interconnect_tap","args":{"link":"A","day":27}}

{"thinking":"Cluster A’s measured peer traffic is consistent with low-communication training and is about 1,000 times the typical inference rate. Probe several nodes across the recorded batch allocation on day 27 to check for training signatures. The readings apply only to the chips the operator presents.","action":"chip_probe","args":{"nodes":["A-0501","A-0640","A-0780","A-0920","A-1060","A-1200"],"hour":634}}

{"thinking":"Sable shares a director and address with Borealis, so its invoice confirmation carries little independent weight. Check F1 on day 16 for a recurring power signature on a second day with elevated GPU-to-GPU traffic. A recurrence would support sustained training activity, while batch periodicity and a smaller training job alongside inference remain plausible.","action":"power_spectrum","args":{"feed":"F1","day":16}}

{"thinking":"F1 showed similar weak power lines on days 18 and 23, and the tap found elevated peer traffic through day 28. A single run, several smaller runs, or training alongside internal batch inference could produce those signals. Recheck three GPUs that previously read as training and two scheduled GPUs that read as inference at hour 640 on day 27. This tests whether the same chips repeatedly show training-like current, while leaving run membership and GPU-hours unresolved.","action":"chip_probe","args":{"nodes":["A-0523","A-0873","A-1037","A-0591","A-1176"],"hour":640}}

{"thinking":"Outbound traffic stayed flat through the F1 surge, which fits both training and internal batch inference. Sample Cluster A on day 20, when F1 showed a steady 0.90 Hz line, to see whether the same elevated peer traffic measured on day 27 was already present. A repeat would strengthen the training hypothesis while leaving the size and continuity of any single run open.","action":"interconnect_tap","args":{"link":"A","day":20}}

{"thinking":"Both GPU feeds and facility overhead rose on days 25–27 and remained elevated on day 28. Check the sealed scheduler records for overlapping allocations, separate jobs, or batch inference that could explain the increase, then test those accounts with independent measurements.","action":"log_escrow","args":{}}

{"thinking":"The tap measured about 10 MB/s on both days 20 and 27, consistent with low-communication training. The day 27 chip readings also leave room for a mixed workload or probe error. Sample five different GPUs across the logged allocation on day 28 to see whether training signatures recur across nodes and days. The probe can only assess the chips presented and cannot link them to a single run.","action":"chip_probe","args":{"nodes":["A-0550","A-0700","A-0850","A-1000","A-1150"],"hour":658}}

{"thinking":"The scheduler records two fine-tunes on different clusters over the same period. The labels and timing fit either two independent jobs or one coordinated run. Measure traffic between clusters on day 26, when both allocations were active, to test whether their GPUs were exchanging training data.","action":"interconnect_tap","args":{"link":"A-B","day":26}}

{"thinking":"All five chips presented on day 28 read as inference. Check F1’s day 28 spectrum to see whether the periodic signal observed on day 20 recurs on a day when every presented chip read as inference. A recurring line would still fit periodic batch inference or an unprobed training workload. A missing line would leave intermittent training possible. Neither result would establish the GPU-hours of a single run.","action":"power_spectrum","args":{"feed":"F1","day":28}}

{"thinking":"The three logged jobs each coincide with a power spike. The steady F2 load on days with no logged job still needs explaining. Check the internet provider’s full-month traffic record for daily demand patterns and for traffic during Kestrel’s batch window. Quiet outbound traffic is consistent with both training and batch inference, so use the traffic record alongside the balance checks to target interconnect sampling.","action":"outbound_traffic","args":{"first_day":1,"last_day":30}}

{"thinking":"Both customers confirmed orders that match the sealed logs. The day 26 tap found little traffic between clusters, which supports separate runs but covers only one day and the listed links. Run the fixed balance checks to see whether the recorded allocations account for the metered power increase and whether any other days warrant investigation.","action":"balance_checks","args":{}}

{"thinking":"Cluster A’s sampled peer traffic was already about 10 MB/s before the F1 load surge, so that rate does not identify the recorded batch job. Check F1’s day 17 spectrum to see whether a similar periodic line also predates the surge. A similar line would support an existing source. If the line is absent, the day 20 and 28 signals still fit either periodic batch inference or training during the surge.","action":"power_spectrum","args":{"feed":"F1","day":17}}

{"thinking":"Both customers confirmed orders that match the scheduler records, and the balance checks account for the metered load. The day 26 tap supports separate runs. Sample the listed links between clusters on day 25, when both jobs began, to test for exchanges during startup that the day 26 measurement could have missed.","action":"interconnect_tap","args":{"link":"A-B","day":25}}

{"thinking":"Day 12’s high GPU-to-GPU traffic and 0.79 Hz power line support training on Cluster B. Check F2 on day 27, when the same unexplained load persisted, for a nearby frequency. A match would support testing for a sustained run with a same-day tap and live chip probe. Separate runs or periodic equipment could also produce similar lines.","action":"power_spectrum","args":{"feed":"F2","day":27}}

{"thinking":"F1 showed a steady 0.44 Hz line on day 26. Check F2 on the same day for a similar or distinct rhythm. A match would warrant checking whether the lines track each other across days or also appear when the fine-tunes are inactive.","action":"power_spectrum","args":{"feed":"F2","day":26}}
